# The Problem

A learner who wants a hands-on tutorial for a specific R package has two options: search the web and hope, or read the vignette, which explains but does not exercise. An instructor who wants to reuse a tutorial has to find it, check the license, check that it still runs, and adapt its build. A package author who wants to offer an interactive tutorial has to learn a toolchain and wire up publishing. All three do this alone.

The tools changed in the last three years. learnr made R Markdown tutorials with exercises, hints and quizzes, but each tutorial needs a Shiny process, so it runs locally or on a Shiny server [@learnr]. learnr has had one CRAN release since September 2023, its request for webR support (issue 766, March 2023) has no maintainer reply, and Posit retired its learnr-based Primers in December 2023. In their place, quarto-live from the r-wasm project at Posit runs R and Python in the browser through WebAssembly and provides exercises with blanks, hints, solutions, setup chunks and grading [@quartolive]. learnr2 adds learnr-style scaffolding and quizzes on top of it. tutorizeR converts existing lessons into learnr or quarto-live tutorials [@tutorizer]. R-universe builds WebAssembly binaries for every CRAN and Bioconductor package it tracks, so a browser tutorial can load DESeq2 [@ooms2023]. Execution without a server is solved.

Discovery, metadata and publishing are not. Three things are missing, checked on 2026-09-26.

1. There is no index of R tutorials. The learnr gallery is a page maintained by Posit. The Swirl Course Network is a directory for one console tool whose last release was in 2020. learnr2's `available_tutorials()` lists tutorials installed on the user's machine. Nothing spans them, and nothing is machine-readable.
2. There is no metadata standard for a tutorial. A tutorial cannot state, in a form a program can read, which packages it teaches, the level, the expected time, the license, and the R and package versions it was last checked against. Without that an index cannot filter, and a reader cannot tell a fresh tutorial from a stale one.
3. There is no template that publishes a browser-run tutorial with Bioconductor packages. Every author writes the GitHub Action, discovers that Bioconductor packages need the r-universe repository, and solves the same rendering problems. Bioconductor's Training Committee maintains Carpentries lessons for bulk RNA-seq and single cell analysis, and I found no browser-run companion for any of them.

The Carpentries Lab shows that a community can review lessons in the open [@carpentrieslab2022], and the ISC funded tooling for consistent teaching materials in 2018. Neither covers short, package-level tutorials that run in the browser. Solving this gives learners one place to search, instructors a way to reuse with confidence, package authors a publishing path that takes an afternoon, and maintainers a view of which packages have teaching material and which do not.
